# vendor/art/the_end — the credits card's lettering

> **Provenance rests on a statement, not on evidence.** The lettering this
> traces was generated by ChatGPT at the project owner's request, and the
> trace was made in the same session and committed by the owner. There is no
> upstream to match against and no generator here that reproduces it. What IS
> checkable is that it is not a copy of a published typeface — a font ships
> outlines, this ships open centrelines — and that everything derived from it
> downstream is deterministic over exactly these bytes. Full statement:
> [`docs/92` §5.1b](../../../docs/92_provenance_audit.md).

One SVG: a **traced centreline** of a monoline cursive "The End", used by the
`aurora` rail as the pen path its writing follows.

| file | what it is |
|---|---|
| `the_end_traced_strokes.svg` | 23 open polylines in a 1672×941 viewBox, stroked white on black, no fills. Not a font, not an outline — a **skeleton**: one polyline per stroke fragment, at the centre of the ink |

## Provenance

**The lettering it traces was generated by ChatGPT**, at the project owner's
request, as a reference for what the letterforms should look like; the SVG
here is a trace of that reference, produced in the same session and committed
by the owner. It is therefore not a scan or a copy of any published typeface,
and it is not third-party pack art of the kind the other directories here
hold — it is recorded in this file because *where a byte came from* is the
question `vendor/art/` exists to answer, and "we made it, with a tool" is an
answer that has to be written down rather than assumed. See
[`docs/92`](../../../docs/92_provenance_audit.md).

## Why a trace at all

Four hand-authored passes at these letters produced four different
misreadings — "Nha Ewel", "Merval", and "Emel" twice. The cause was one shape:
a cursive capital **T** is a near-horizontal BAR with a steep riser CROSSING
it, and a curve drawn from memory keeps producing a stem with a peak, which
the eye reads as an N. Tracing settles the shapes; `tools/write_on.py` does
the rest.

## What the trace's own geometry says

Measured off the reference image by column-scanning it: baseline y = 522,
x-height 52 px, ascenders reaching y = 341 — so the ascender is **3.5
x-heights** and the whole word, swash to swash, is **25 x-heights wide and 3.8
tall**. Those proportions, not a chosen size, are what place the word inside
the black band under the cliff.

The fragments are in **no drawing order**, and the file's `stroke-NNN` ids are
not one. `tools/write_on.py` recovers a hand from the graph: twelve nodes have
odd degree, so no single unbroken trail covers it and six is the fewest that
can — and six nodes have degree ONE, which are exactly the free terminals
visible in the reference (the entry tip, the T's oval tail, the T's stem foot,
the E's tail, the n's head, the exit tip). Each trail is begun at a terminal
and carries on through junctions by least bend.
